title: Event Sourcing Pros and Cons
description: Evaluate the trade-offs of event sourcing, understand its costs, and learn when to choose it over traditional persistence.

data.text: Event sourcing is a powerful pattern, but it is not free. It changes how you think about data, debugging, testing, and team onboarding. Understanding the trade-offs helps you decide whether event sourcing is the right tool for your problem. There is no universal answer, but there are clear signals for when it pays off.

data.title: Pros
items: Complete audit trail by default; every change is a recorded fact.
Temporal queries: you can reconstruct state at any point in time.
Event replay makes debugging, migration testing, and analytics easier.
Loose coupling between services through shared event streams.
Event schemas can evolve without breaking existing data.

data.title: Cons
items: Steeper learning curve for teams new to the pattern.
Eventual consistency in read models complicates UX design.
Schema evolution requires discipline across all consumers.
Snapshot and replay logic adds operational complexity.
Debugging requires reading event streams instead of current state.

cards.title: Event Sourcing
cards.description: Stores every state change as an immutable event. Current state is derived by replay.

cards.title: Traditional CRUD
cards.description: Stores only current state. Updates overwrite previous values.

data.text: Choose event sourcing when your domain requires a complete history, when temporal queries are a core feature, or when you are building a system of collaborating microservices that need a shared source of truth. Financial ledgers, insurance policies, and supply-chain trackers are classic examples. If your application is a simple CRUD app with no audit requirements, a traditional database is almost always the better choice.

data.title: Quick Check: Is Event Sourcing Right for You?
data.content: Ask these questions before committing to the pattern.

data.title: Start with Events, Not Necessarily an Event Store
data.text: You can publish domain events from a traditional database without fully adopting event sourcing. This gives you many benefits of loose coupling and auditability while keeping the simplicity of a relational database. Adopt full event sourcing only when you have outgrown this approach.

data.caption: Decision factors for choosing event sourcing

items.question: Can I combine event sourcing with a traditional database?
items.answer: Yes. Many systems use a traditional database for read models and an event store for the write side. The two stores serve different purposes and can coexist without conflict.

items.question: Is event sourcing worth it for a small team?
items.answer: It depends. Event sourcing adds operational overhead. For a small team with a simple domain, a traditional database with event publishing is often sufficient. Adopt event sourcing when your team is comfortable with the complexity and your domain clearly benefits from it.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Event sourcing gives you audit trails, temporal queries, and reliable replay.
It introduces eventual consistency, schema evolution challenges, and operational overhead.
Choose it when the domain genuinely requires a complete history.
Start with domain events before committing to a full event-sourced architecture.
data.takeaway: Event sourcing is a tool for complex domains. Use it when the benefits outweigh the costs.
